I am grateful to the minister for his clarification and I will try to resist the temptation of following him into a discussion of unemployment. I have here a quotation from the Prime Minister's statement in Regina of February 13, 1958-it is from the Regina Leader-Post-in which he talks about a work program, including roads, of $1,185 million in order to assure jobs. It was a work program to assure jobs in so far as the 4,000 miles are concerned. Now the minister says he had in mind not only roads in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories, but roads south leading to the north and access roads to the resources of the north. With a little bit more time I am sure the minister could find a good many more roads than even 4,000 miles of them because you could make a case for any road south being of value in opening up the north or leading in that direction.
The Prime Minister did not make any such suggestion as that in his broadcast, the text of which I have before me, and in which he talks about a road building program in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. He said the program was 4,000 miles and there it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext: Again, Mr. Chairman, I think this is just merely a matter of-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I am glad the minister has opened up discussion in the field of the roads to resources program at this point because it gives me an opportunity to touch on an aspect of it which the Leader of the Opposition has perhaps been too kind to take the opportunity of discussing. Since the minister today raised this subject of roads to resources, I should like to ask him why he is having so much difficulty in northern Ontario in getting co-operation from premier Frost and this lovely government at Queen's Park. very little work has been done on any of them? Where is the breakdown? Is Premier Frost not co-operating with him or is he not co-operating with Premier Frost? I think he

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have two points which I should like to cover here. One refers to a point raised by the Leader of the Opposition and the other to a point raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. In my view both these gentlemen have been trying to make political mileage-

subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext: It was the Prime Minister who was trying to make political mileage.

subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext:
-in trying to pick picayune holes in statements made by the Prime Minister and others concerning this northern development roads' program.
I have had my files sent down from my office and I have in front of me two statements made by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate talks about making statements to the Canadian people which are not accurate. He should listen to a little bit of that advice himself, and so should his leader. They talk about misadvising and misleading the Canadian people on these things. They talk about giving the Canadian people facts which are not facts.
Here is the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition in Vancouver on September 27, 1958:
Diefenbaker's promise of a billion dollar public works program in the Arctic is the phoniest promise ever made in Canadian history.
The Prime Minister, in this house, in any campaign or anywhere else in this country, never said there was going to be a billion dollar public works program in the Arctic. He was describing a national public works program, included in which was a program of northern development roads.
If that statement of the Leader of the Opposition is not misrepresenting what the Prime Minister went to the country with, I do not know what is a misrepresenting statement. The Leader of the Opposition made another statement in Edmonton, Alberta, on October 4, 1958:
Canadians have been hoodwinked by the Progressive Conservative government's promise of northern development.
That also is an extremely misrepresenting statement, because far from hoodwinking Canadians, the figures which I filed in this committee on May 4 show that in the period 1952-57 the total expenditures of the northern administration branch of this department
Supply-Northern Affairs were $29,906,075, compared with the period 1957-62 in which these expenditures amount to $137,600,472.
That is not a phony promise, as was expressed in the statement of the Leader of the Opposition in Edmonton on October 4. That is not hoodwinking the Canadian people. Does the hon. gentleman think it is hoodwinking the Canadian people to say to them, "We will build these development roads to develop the nation's resources"? All he has to do is consider the tungsten mine which is being developed. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources pointed out that it is the only tungsten mine in Canada and will commence production in November, 1962. The largest single tungsten deposit in the world-it will place Canada in the position of being the world's largest single supplier of this very rare and valuable metal in the race for space.
This is what these roads are accomplishing. These are not roads from igloo to igloo. I would point out to the hon. gentleman once again that he has not yet answered my question as to whether he still adheres to his igloo to igloo statement. I do not think he does, but I should like him to admit it.

Ottawa-The federal government hopes Canadians will be able to participate heavily in northern oil development-but it isn't making any guarantees.
Supply-Northern Affairs
Its hopes are contained in a loosely-drawn set of regulations governing Canadian participation made public Wednesday, which even resources minister Alvin Hamilton admits are open to various interpretations.
"Any lawyer could tear holes in them," he said.
He explained the government sought to avoid overly-restrietive rules-
And apparently overly-restrietive statistics, too.

The regulations were drawn after more than a year's study, 30-odd full-scale cabinet meetings, and scores of conferences among government officials.

A lease shall not be granted-to a corporation incorporated outside of Canada, or-to a corporation unless the minister is satisfied that the shares of the corporation are listed on a recognized Canadian stock exchange and that Canadians will have an opportunity of assisting in the financing and ownership.

Thank you very much. I have been interested in the artistic, cultural, and social development of our northern citizens, particularly Eskimos to whom the minister's department has given great assistance. I feel the minister and his departmental officials should be complimented in this regard.
We often hear criticism in Canada regarding the influence of other Canadians on Eskimo traditions and life, and I can refer specifically to Eskimo designs, stone and bone carvings, and so forth. I understand that the situation was in a state of flux as times changed, and, that if it were not for the fact that direction was given to these people, these arts might truly have died out with the passage of years. These artistic talents, on the part of Eskimos, have been manifested in recent years through the production of stone carvings, and unusual prints, stimulated by the officers of the minister's department. These have created a great impression in the artistic world in this country and, in fact, in many lands of the globe. The recent

printing method which has been developed may prove even more international in artistic merit than the earlier carvings. Creative work with fur, leather and other materials has been encouraged and I feel it should be carried even further. The recognition and independence these achievements give as well as the remuneration to the Eskimo artists, are most important. As a result of this remuneration the Eskimos is becoming more varied in outlook and I think this is evidenced by the fact that the Eskimos have hired at least one individual from the south to advise them in regard to the sale and distribution of their artistic works.
In addition, the introduction of such things as one room houses for the Eskimos which have been developed by the department in recent years are most interesting. I understand that there are to be more than a thousand of these sent to the north in the months and years ahead, to be purchased largely by the Eskimos themselves. I think this is a move in the right direction. The best of the old ways must be maintained, but some changes must be planned, and brought about.
The employment of Eskimos in hospitals and in various services as mechanics, in the north, is a healthy sign. The new vocational school at Yellowknife costing, I believe, some $3 million is an interesting development and should give an opportunity to those northern citizens to educate themselves, to acquire additional skills to develop fully the very great natural talents they have. As the minister has pointed out, the people of the north are Canadians, and have every right to equal facilities and opportunities.
I understand that the education of Eskimo children is not now so much a problem when the facilities are there; that they are able to bridge the gap between civilizations to a very great extent. The problem may perhaps lie more with the older group of 15 to 30 years of age, and older still, to try to give them the skills and opportunities to make a living in a changing world. It is commendable that this year 60 per cent of the Eskimos of school age are attending school, compared with only 16 per cent three years ago.
I would say again that the efforts of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, of the minister and of the industrial division of the department deserve the highest commendation.
As far as the art forms which have created such a stir around the world are concerned,
I would only say that the necessity for maintaining the highest standards possible both in materials and designs must always be kept in mind. As well, a close examination might continually be given to methods of sales and distribution of these products. From time to
Supply-Northern Affairs time it has come to my notice, largely by rumour, although from reputable people, indeed, that numbers of these products have gone forth from Canada to Great Britain, to Europe and the United States by various means. This may well be right and proper but I do feel that the first opportunity for acquiring these creations should be given to Canadians themselves.

It was a film produced by the national film board dealing with the subject of building in the north, and it gave a very interesting review of the specialized construction techniques that had been developed as a result of the experience in building the new Inuvik community.

These are just a few of the studies that are under way in the natural history field and they strike me as being quite impressive. At six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I mentioned the fact that I had a few questions I wished to direct to the minister. In so doing, I do not wish to repeat the arguments I put forward on April 21 when we examined these matters. However, it seems to me that the minister has left unanswered some of the questions I put to him at that time. I should like to point out that I am not pursuing these matters in any political sense but only in the hope that we can perhaps together focus public attention on this particular problem. I am referring specifically to the deficit in our travel account.
I would refer you, Mr. Chairman, to two figures in the Bank of Canada report which shows a steady worsening of this situation, from that in 1950 where we had a surplus in that travel account of some $49 million to that in 1960, ten years later, where we had a deficit of $215 million. As I say, this situation, of course, is worsening-as is proven- and it will be changed only by vigorous and imaginative action that recognizes the seriousness of this problem. Concerning the travel account between ourselves and the United States, there is a deficit of something of the order of $100 million. I hope to have something to say about that matter a little bit later.
Further in this regard may I say that I was disappointed to hear the minister's brief report on the action being taken to recognize the importance of the European tourist spending. From what the minister has said, the situation appears to be this. Last year they had a look at it; this year they are having a look at what they had a look at last year, and next year they may take some action. Thus three years are wasted when we could be taking some real advantage of the resurgence of the economy in Europe. I noted also

Supply-Northern Affairs that the minister referred particularly to some proposed action in the United Kingdom. I hope he can give us some more information about that matter and about what action is proposed to be taken on the continent itself.
The other day I mentioned the matter of the degree of spending by the Canadian government as compared with that of some other countries. I do not wish to repeat the things I said the other day, but tonight I should like to refer briefly to the matter and compare our situation with that of Mexico. In 1960 the Mexican government more than doubled their spending on tourist promotion. They boosted it to 24.4 million pesos from 10 million pesos in '59 and there was a further increase in the 1961 budget. They are spending approximately $2 million. When one takes off the administrative costs from the Mexican allotment and does the same thing with regard to the allotment here in Canada, we find that we are spending a similar amount. When we compare our national budget with the national budget of Mexico, we find that ours is roughly $6.5 billion while theirs is $1 billion. It can therefore be seen that the Mexican government are spending six and one half times the amount of money that we are spending in this country. I would also remind the committee that this money is being mostly directed at the United States market and with some effect. In 1960 United States tourist spending amounted to $200 million plus another $100 million at the border.
Another aspect of the matter is, of course, the encouragement of more Canadians to spend their vacations in Canada. As I pointed out the other day, if one in six Canadian tourists spent his vacation in Canada, this deficit would be wiped out.
I think a strong program is needed to bring this matter to the attention of our people and also a strong program directed at our great potential markets. I very seldom in this chamber recommend the spending of more money by the government, but I believe the need in this field is very obvious. The returns are very rewarding. I do not think we can afford to ignore this situation any longer.
I should like to hear specifically what the government plans are because, from the results being obtained, it is quite clear that the present activity is not good enough, as is proven by these facts. I should like to hear from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in replying to the comments of the hon. member the other day I suggested he was far too pessimistic in his observations on trends in the tourist industry in Canada.
I pointed out that for the first time our tourist industry occupies the No. 2 position

in terms of earning export dollars. I think that in itself is a move in a positive direction. We have occupied the No. 3 position for a number of years now, and our present position indicates that we are moving in the desired direction.
The hon. member made some point of comparing the Canadian situation with the Mexican situation. I do not think the two are quite comparable. For example, the climate of Mexico is somewhat warmer for a longer period of time and the tourist has access to the Mexican tourist market for almost a 12-month period.
The hon. member also quoted figures pointing out the growing number of United States dollars which are spent in Mexico. I understand that a good proportion of this expenditure is in the border towns, where extensive gambling operations are carried on. We do not have a similar activity in Canada, and from that standpoint I do not think the two countries are comparable. I think the percentage of United States dollars earned from that activity is 65 per cent of the total.
The hon. member also made a point about the increased allotment of funds by the Mexican government in tourist promotion. There is a special explanation for this. I understand there is a $3 per head tax on all tourists entering Mexico and this is applied to the cost of tourist promotion. A large percentage of the sum the hon. member mentioned is derived from that source.
We are on the verge of what we may call an explosion in tourist population-we use this phrase generally about a population explosion-and I think within the next few years we will see this situation developing in the tourist industry in Canada. The trend is already in that direction.
The tourist bureau has up to the present time devoted most of its attention to cultivating the United States tourist, for a very obvious reason. Here is a large population with a high standard of living right at our own doorstep and we feel this is the most lucrative source from which to increase our tourist dollars.
I am very happy to inform the committee that since 1958 the trend that had been under way up to that point, of a deficiency in terms of the relative position of United States dollars spent in Canada and Canadian dollars spent in the United States, is moving in the right direction. The imbalance in 1958 was $104 million; in 1959 it was $97 million, and last year it was down to $79 million. I think this is a very encouraging trend and suggests that the activities of the tourist bureau are paying off at an accelerated rate.
I think I should also point out, Mr. Chairman, that one of the reasons for the larger

expenditure of Canadian dollars in the United States market arises from the fact that Canadians have been in the habit of making visits to the United States for the specific purpose of going on a shopping spree. It has been a favourite Canadian pastime to take a week end or a week or so for the specific purpose of shopping in the United States. Canadians have been under the impression that goods in the United States are cheaper and perhaps more varied than they are in Canada.
My colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has recently been making speeches on this subject encouraging Canadians to shop at home. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has been pointing out that goods available here are equally as good and as cheap as those to be purchased in any part of the United States. I am sure the enthusiasm he is devoting to imparting this message will have its effect on the problem upon which the hon. member for Nipissing dwelt at some length tonight.
We must also take into account the fact that a good many elderly, retired Canadians go south in the winter and are actually in residence in the warmer climates of the southern states for months at a time. This involves a considerable outlay of Canadian dollars.
I appreciate the hon. member's desire to encourage tourism as quickly and as aggressively as possible. I assure him that this is precisely what we are doing. If the hon. member has followed the tourist promotional theme during the past few years he will have noticed that it is one of getting to know Canada better.
We feel we now have more effective representation in the United States; we feel this is having its effect. I understand we have been promoting the federal-provincial tourist conference for the past 15 years. This conference was first brought together for the purpose of getting closer collaboration between the provinces and the federal government in making a concerted assault on the United States' tourist market potential.
The province of Quebec, for example, has special attractions for United States tourists and I am happy to say that this province has one of the most effective tourist promotional campaigns. They have also pioneered in encouraging Canadians to spend their holidays in Canada and there has been a noticeable increase in visits by Canadians from the maritimes, Ontario and other parts of Canada to the province of Quebec.
I do not know whether there is anything else I can add to the points which have already been stressed, except to refer to the potential in the European market. Up to the present time this potential has not been specifically tapped or promoted by our tourist
Supply-Northern Affairs bureau. The trend in balance of payments here has been moving against Canada. Our citizens have been visiting the United Kingdom and Europe in larger numbers than the number of visitors to Canada from those two areas.
It is for this very reason that we feel the time has come for a direct assault on this market, especially in view of the increased prosperity in Europe and the United Kingdom and the tendency on the part of these people to travel more than they have in the past.
I appreciate the support the hon. member for Nipissing has given to this matter. I can assure him that I, as minister, and the officials of the tourist bureau are entirely in sympathy with the representations he has made. All in all I think we can say that tourism is moving in the right direction. The figure for expenditures in Canada last year was $417 million. That is the highest on record and all I can say is: as far as we are concerned, that and better will do.

speechtext:
In spite of all the fine things the minister has just said, and I do appreciate them, the fact does remain that the situation-the deficit on our travel account- is worsening each year. I can only hope that through all the people who are working in the tourist industry in this country this problem can be met.
I should like to ask the minister if there is anything new in reference to the proposed United States legislation to restrict the expenditure of American tourists in Canada. I know the hon. gentleman answered this question on a couple of earlier occasions, but I would point out that some time has elapsed since the matter was raised. I think the idea was first suggested by President Kennedy early in February. As to the last word I have, I would refer to a press report which appeared in the London Free Press of April 25. It reads:
Washington (CP)-President Kennedy's proposed reduction in the U.S. tariff-free tourist goods allowance to $100 from $500 was approved by the house ways and means committee yesterday.
That was on April 25. The report goes on to say:
But a committee spokesman said that Kennedy's request to maintain the reduction for four years was opposed by the committee, which will offer a new bill to the house of representatives today cutting the authority to two years until July 1, 1963. Kennedy wanted the authority until April 1, 1965.
I wonder if the minister has anything new to report on this subject and, if not, whether he would seize any opportunity which may present itself when President Kennedy, perhaps the outstanding tourist to visit Canada this year, is in our capital.

I am certain I have acquainted them with the Canadian viewpoint on this important subject. '

In connection with this same matter I should like to point out the seriousness with which some of the businessmen in Canada who are connected with the tourist industry view this proposed change. I would remind the minister that when our Prime Minister visited Washington, on February 20 I think it was, he indicated, according to a Canadian press report emanating from Washington, that he had heard of no objection in Canada.
I wish to refer to only one of the news items I have here, although I have several. I should like to refer to a report which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of February 7 according to which Mr. James Hughes, executive vice president of the greater Vancouver tourist association called on the federal government to seek exemption for Canada if congress passes the scheme. Also concerned, according to the same report, was Mr. E. L. Harrison, president of the Vancouver board of trade. He foresaw a threat to the provincial economy and launched a fact finding study of the situation. Mr. Hughes is reported to have said that such a move by the United States would cut retail spending in British Columbia by a third and mean a loss of $5 million a year. Thus, without pursuing this matter further, I again express the hope that most earnest representations can be made in the appropriate quarter. Perhaps I may read one further excerpt from this report in the Vancouver Sun, a statement attributed to Mr. Hughes:
If Ottawa takes the position that this will have no effect on the Canadian economy it will be wishful thinking.
So I think there is ample proof of the feeling across the country that such a move would mean a great loss to Canada if it were ever implemented as originally announced back in February.
Before I sit down, may I ask whether the minister can report on the activities of the tourist bureau office in New York since its move from 49th Street to Canada House on Fifth Avenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: I have just obtained the information from one of the officials. He informs me that inquiries are up from 60,800 to some 70,900 since the move was made, which indicates that the situation has been considerably improved.

speechtext: I thank the minister for that reply. Perhaps I am being partisan here, but it seems to me that the view advanced by the Liberals on earlier occasions-I am referring particularly to January, 1958, when we supported this move and when so many hon. members who are now sitting opposite rejected it in principle-has been justified by events. I am glad to hear the minister say the rewards have been encouraging, because it seems to me that this move from 49th Street to Fifth Avenue, which is really the show street, was certainly a good move. I am glad to hear the minister confirm the wisdom of making it.

The tourist industry is an important and growing industry in Kootenay West and consequently a good number of my constituents are interested in the activities of the Canadian travel bureau.
Before raising a few questions I want to say that I check the United States papers and I check the Canadian papers and keep in fairly close touch with what the travel bureau is doing. I think it is doing an excellent job and I think its work has improved in recent years. No doubt that is the result of experience and of the recommendations of the committee on mines, forests and waters when the estimates of this bureau are discussed and members present their views and put forward suggestions.
Would the minister inform the house whether arrangements are being made for the establishment of an office in San Francisco? This question was originally brought up in 1959. At that time the minister informed the house and informed me personally that the government did not see fit to establish an office there because of budget requirements and things of that sort. I should like the minister to inform the committee whether any consideration is now being given to establishing an office in San Francisco. This is a very important location. I think one of our former cabinet ministers has been put out to pasture in San Francisco.

This one was rather more fortunate. I do not know whether that would be altogether sufficient, but I should like the minister to inform us whether consideration has been given to that suggestion. I have been

asked to raise these matters in the committee by the tourist resorts association in my district.
During the discussion of the estimates a year or so ago there was reference made to the animated advertisement sign in Times Square, which was reputed to be the first, as far as publicity was concerned on the part of the tourist bureau, in perhaps any country. At that time the minister took a very optimistic view and approach to this animated advertisement. I should like the minister to inform the committee if that sign is still operating, and if there has been any check made as to the result.
I have been asked to inquire, regarding my third point, by a number of tourist resort operators in my district, and the number is growing every year. This operation provides an excellent opportunity, for an individual with limited capital who is willing to work over a period of years, to build up a nice litle business. I have been asked to point out that these resort operators are of the opinion that the Kootenays are somewhat overlooked in the advertisements directed to the potential tourist market. In looking at a United States paper recently I found there was quite a spread given to the advertisement of the Okanagan. The Okanagan is a very good fruit growing district; it is a lovely valley, but is not as scenic as the Kootenays. The only mention of the Kootenays, which appeared in that United States paper, was a statement to the effect that an individual would also find much of that which is to be desired in the Kootenays.
Mr. Chairman, the Kootenays are the Switzerland of Canada. There exist there unparalleled fishing, hunting, boating and hundreds of lovely beaches. There are seven excellent hot springs which are developed, or partially developed, as well as a number of small ones which have not been developed to date. The existence of these things provides a mecca for tourists, and I should like to impress this upon the minister and his officials this evening, because I feel they do not realize the opportunities for enjoyment that exist in the Kootenays along the lines I have mentioned. As a result I urge that further consideration be given, in advertising, to this garden of Eden of Canada.
I should also like the minister, when he is replying, to give us some information in regard to the department's policy on advertising in Canadian and United States papers and periodicals. I should like to know whether this is done on a rotation basis advertising one part of Canada one month and another part the next and what type of periodical is employed for this purpose. I should also like to know what psychology is used in the
Supply-Northern Affairs writing of these advertisements and whether they are written by government travel bureau officials or by private advertising firms.
I should be very pleased if the minister will answer these questions, and can assure him, if he does so, that I will be quiet for the rest of the evening while these estimates are being considered.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies, I should like to call his attention, and the attention of his officials, to those glowing remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West, and inform this committee that those remarks apply equally to every constituency in British Columbia. British Columbia is really a tourist's paradise.
I am very pleased to note that a former cabinet minister is now in San Francisco in order to promote tourist travel, but I would suggest that the minister will be able to find very competent civil servants to staff the office, and will not be able to find any more cabinet ministers in British Columbia who are looking for jobs. I suggest one is probably enough in San Francisco.
As I understand the situation, his department is not using the direct mail method of inducing United States tourists to visit resorts in British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Ontario, the maritimes and across Canada, but I would suggest this is perhaps another method which would be useful. I would suspect that, because of the minister's love for the north, and the development of access roads to the north, it will soon become an equally attractive tourist paradise, and I refer to areas such as the Cariboo in British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The opening of these areas will provide to tourists visiting these areas the attraction of adventure of a type which will not be found in the more settled parts to the south.
In view of the present balance of trade with the United States it would be very detrimental to the tourist industry if anything were done in the way of advertising which would restrict the flow of tourists from the United States. Trade in a tourist sense has been and is in favour of the United States, and I do not think this should be so. The tourist trade balance should be on Canada's credit side, and I hope the minister and his officials will work to that end.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext:
Some of our best national parks are located in mountainous areas, and we feel that with the bureau operating in San Francisco there will be a dramatic increase in the number of tourists flowing into Canada from this part of the United States.
As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South, one of our most attractive tourist regions is, in our opinion, the wilderness of the Canadian north. Because of its geographic location it is anticipated that the greatest portion of the increase in the number of tourists coming to Canada will come from that area served by the San Francisco bureau. In anticipation of this influx of tourists the national historic sites and monuments branch has been active. As I mentioned in the committee the other day, we hope to have the Klondike festival operating for the 1962 tourist season. This festival is a revival of the romance of the trail of '98 and will be located in the Grand Palace auditorium in Dawson City. All these projects are designed to create greater drawing power on the United States tourist potential.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has made some inquiry as to the impact of the animated sign in Times Square in the city of New York, but I am afraid it is impossible to draw any categorical conclusions concerning its effectiveness. All one can say is that it is directed toward millions of people every day, and its effectiveness is shown by the increase of 40 per cent in the number of inquiries made at the New York office since the sign went into operation.
I think perhaps the hon. member himself may be able to draw some conclusions on this score if he attends the showing of the new animated films which will be held in the railway committee room on the evening of May 23 during the recess between the afternoon and the evening sittings. We are extending an invitation to all members of the house to be present. We feel this is even a better effort than last year because the drawings have been done by the eminent Canadian animationist, Mr. McLaren, who has gained an international reputation in the field of animated cartoons.
The hon. member also asked some questions about the nature of our advertising program. Recently the Canadian government travel bureau initiated media studies of its own which gather statistical data on a scientific basis and which make it possible for them to determine which media have had


the most significant impact with regard to tourist promotion; but perhaps I can give a little general information on this score which might be helpful to the committee.
Over the past four years a conscientious effort has been made to improve the image of Canada to show it as not only a place for outdoor recreation, sports and sightseeing but a country with the second highest standard of living in the world with good resorts, hotels and restaurants. Particular emphasis is laid on festivals and events like the Stratford festival, the Vancouver festival, the Calgary stampede, the Canadian national exhibition, the Gaelic Mod and others. Increasing use is made of the more influential publications which have a high prestige value.
In 1961, the bureau plans to continue advertising designed to create a broader image of Canada to those citizens who have the means to travel and who live near enough to be logical tourist prospects for Canada.
The new major theme in our advertising in 1961 will be the trans-Canada highway, which has now reached the stage of near-completion, which will permit us to feature it as a major attraction for the 70 million people of the United States who are owners of automobiles.
The newspaper campaign in 1961 will use photographs rather than drawings, as was done in 1960. Larger advertisements of 1,000 lines will appear in major newspapers to attract attention by dominating the page. Plans are also under way to streamline the lists of newspapers to remove non-productive publications.
Just before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to the special Atlantic provinces campaign. The special Atlantic provinces campaign was inaugurated in 1957 as a special economic measure to help the four Atlantic provinces, on the grounds that these provinces were more economically depressed than other provinces. Since that time the impact of the tourist industry in the maritime provinces has been moving onward and upward. Indeed, it was in that area of Canada that tourism first occupied the No. 2 position.

I was very much interested in hearing the minister speak about the tourist bureau functioning now in New York and the one to be opened in San Francisco. Have we any tourist bureaux in the middle west, in Chicago or Minneapolis? In this area there are 30 million potential tourists. To my mind one of the greatest attractions is northwestern Ontario. People travel from Minneapolis up to Duluth, Minnesota and on to Fort William and Port Arthur. To complete the southern tour of lake Superior there is a highway of

approximately 1,200 to 1,300 miles which circles the entire lake from the Sault, down through the lakehead to Minnesota, and Michigan. I wish to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that this is one of the most scenic highways in North America. The scenic splendour is unsurpassed even by the magnitude of the rocky mountain area of British Columbia mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South and the area mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Nothing can compare with the splendour of the lake Superior area.
Is the minister's department considering doing anything about some promotional work to attract United States tourists to northwestern Ontario and inveigling them to take the southern tour? It is one of the features of northwestern Ontario. As a matter of fact, it can be classed as one of the major tourist attractions in Ontario. I urge the minister to give serious consideration to some promotional work in the middle west of the United States to attract tourists into northwestern Ontario. This may not be a national project to the extent that it benefits largely the province of Ontario, but indirectly, it benefits the entire nation. I can assure the minister that the lakehead cities are well provided with facilities to take care of many tourists when they get them, but we do need additional promotional work. The cities themselves are doing considerable work along that line; they are spending money on their own. People in the business are also doing the same thing, but we do require the assistance of the government, and I urge the minister to give some serious consideration to this part of the province of Ontario which richly deserves assistance.

Supply-Northern Affairs been placed in the hands of most hon. members. It was published just over a month ago and depicts the tourist attractions of all sections of the trans-Canada highway. It was rather difficult to obtain figures on the anticipated spending for Inuvik but I think we have them as completely as possible in the short time that has been available. As of June 15, 1956, the first over-all estimate of the total cost for moving the items at Aklavik and, second, the cost of the new and enlarged installations at Inuvik, was as follows: Removal costs were $2,190,000 and new construction was $21,092,500, which gives a total of $23,282,527 or pretty close to the final figure. This, however, did not include the Department of National Defence establishments and the engineering fees. The actual cost including these other factors was $34,045,970. The additional costs amounting to $10.8 million were made up as follows: Department of National Defence base, $900,000; airport terminal, $849,682; laundry and freezers, $515,000; fire hall, $100,000; engineering fees, $92,000, which comes to a total of $2,456,682. The cost increases were due to the larger size of facilities and the increases in costs from the time of the original estimates, amounting in all to $8.3 million. I understand there are complete details on this subject in the proceedings of the committee on mines, forests and waters for 1958 but I hope that this brief survey provides the necessary information.
With reference to the priorities situation in the Arctic, I understand that prior to the coming into effect of the Canada oil and gas regulations on April 13, 1960, there were 142 million acres under priority. Following promulgation of the Canada oil and gas regulations 43J million acres were taken up under oil and gas exploration permits. The reason for the differential in the figures arises, of course, from the fact that the Canadian participation clauses meant that some of the Americans who had established priorities did not pick them up and convert them into exploratory permits. As the hon. member knows, the policy of the government is to protect Canada's heritage for Canadians, and I think this has been demonstrated in the figures I have revealed to the committee.

Supply-Northern Affairs of the minister to the Century 21 exposition to be held next year in Seattle, Washington, when that city will play host to the nations of the world. While that exhibition is in progress there I should like to feel that we could send some major units -for example, the searchlight tattoo-to Seattle, Washington, It could do a fine job in that area. Thousands of people saw the searchlight tattoo when it was put on in British Columbia. I should like to feel that the officials of the Canadian government travel bureau would make an effort to see whether this really fine Canadian product could be sent to Seattle in order to entertain world visitors there. Because of the value of the tourist trade to us in British Columbia, I should also like to feel that the minister might encourage the Prime Minister to be in Seattle, Washington, at the time of the exposition. I understand that an invitation has already been extended to him to be there.
I do not want to pass this particular subject without drawing to the attention of the minister the fact that some 45,000 visitors a day are expected m Seattle, Washington and that there will be more accommodations there than were developed for the Brussels world fair. This will give you some idea of the size of this exposition being staged in Seattle which is a city much like Vancouver, of equal size and in the same location in the Pacific northwest. I therefore hope that the officials of the Canadian government travel bureau will do everything possible to send Canadian shows or Canadian spectacles to the Seattle area because such action will certainly help us in every way possible. It may well be also that special billboards could be put up in Seattle encouraging tourists to come north. It may well be that we could have an animated sign much like the one the travel bureau have erected in Times Square in New York.
May I also say how pleased I am that the government has decided to open up a travel office in the city of San Francisco. I know that at the present time the civil service are trying to secure a person to supervise that

Supply-Northern Affairs office. I should like to urge upon the minister that, if at all possible, the officer who will supervise that office be a person from western Canada. Most of the tourists will be from the Los Angeles and San Francisco bay area. We should like that officer to have an intimate knowledge of everything in the western provinces of Canada. That office will serve us well. It may well be that in the near future, in order to have a slightly more elegant office, the Canadian government could join forces with the provincial government because they are also setting up offices in San Francisco at an early date.
I therefore make two suggestions. One is that we join with the province of British Columbia in having a more elaborate set-up in San Francisco. The second is that we have managing the office in San Francisco an officer who will be from western Canada. I saw the animated sign in Times Square. I thought it was a sound effort. It must be doing a good job. Many people have commented upon it. However, that sign is in, the east. I hope that we can have a similar sign in the Los Angeles area or in the San Francisco area because of the tremendous value to us of the tourist trade in that area.
When you open up the travel bureau office in the bay area, I think it would be a reasonable suggestion that you have many Canadian government officials in that area and also that you take with you a contingent of the R.C.M.P. They put on a colourful show in that area but it would indicate to everyone that Canada is doing something in that area. That is one added suggestion. You will be opening your office, I presume, in July. We could try that also. There is one other matter I should like to draw to the minister's attention. I dealt with it at length yesterday. I refer to the matter of winter tourism. I now have the official report of the engineers who reported to the Canadian Olympic Association. On page 29 of that report they say this-and this is an unbiased report:
The present exodus of skiers from the Vancouver lower mainland to the U.S. for week end and vacation skiing results in the outflow of perhaps $1 million annually which is not counterbalanced by any return visits to British Columbia since there are no facilities available to attract U.S. tourist dollars.
The report goes on to say:
Provided the development required to satisfy the local lower mainland demand were supplied, then it is believed that the international exchange


of tourist dollars would, at least, be balanced, and it might even be possible to achieve a net inflow of tourist dollars to the lower mainland area for skiing purposes.
The report points out that on a typical week end, Seymour, which is a ski area very close to us in Vancouver, receives 6,000 skiers, whereas Mount Baker, a United States resort about 90 miles south of us in Vancouver, receives some 4,000 skiers. It was that situation to which I referred yesterday and it it is my earnest hope that in the foreseeable future something will be done to rectify this situation.

subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext: What about Garibaldi?

subsubtopic: VISIT OF PREMIER OF ISRAEL TO CANADA
speechtext:
In all fairness I must say that the Canadian government has done a fair job in encouraging tourists to come to our area in the summertime. However, I hope much more encouragement can be given, coupled with the building of a proper resort in our area to encourage people in the northwest area of the United States to come to Canada and British Columbia for the winter tourist season.
I was pleased to find that a year ago, for the first time to my knowledge, the Canadian government travel bureau sent pamphlets to an international winter show. I refer in this case to Squaw Valley. Thousands upon thousands of pamphlets were distributed to people who came from all over the world to follow the winter sports events at Squaw Valley.
This was a very good thing and I hope that in the future Canada will have on the grounds of these international sports areas a suitable warming area, if it is in the winter time, which could be called the Canadian area or Canada House. I know that at Squaw Valley the French had a typical and appropriate building, as did Austria and some other countries. We did not plan well enough in advance to have such a building.
We now know that other countries construct this type of building and I hope that at Innsbruck, where the next international winter show will be held, we will have an appropriate warming area so that people who gather at the show can go there, see Canadian wares and pick up Canadian literature.
I also hope we will have a small Canadian pin of very inexpensive construction available at this show. These pins are found everywhere at these international events. I do not think pins of this type would cost more than a cent or two apiece. I am not talking of the type of pin which must be screwed on or affixed to your lapel with other expensive gadgets; I am talking about a pin of simple design, certainly with the maple leaf and the word "Canada" on it which can be pinned

on to one's lapel in some appropriate and simple way. This is so important at these international events and I hope the minister will at an early date get in touch with some *companies or Canadian research institute and have them design an appropriate pin which can be handed out.
I have another point which ties in with government promotion of the tourist industry. British Columbia needs direct air services to southern California to tap the rich source of tourist dollars there. We have no direct carriers into the California area at the present time. If we had carriers, they could fly directly from San Francisco into Vancouver and we could do a better job in bringing tourists into British Columbia.
I feel that we could solve some of our other tourist problems by instituting the type of system the United States government has provided at their ports of entry and airports. One can go through United States customs on the Canadian side and when you de-plane, for example in New York, there are no further delays in the host country.
If we had carriers flying directly into Canada we could open Canadian customs and immigration offices, say in Seattle, and when the traveller arrived in Vancouver there would be no further delay. Delays are encountered at the present time.
If the officials of the Canadian government travel bureau could encourage their counterparts in some of the other government departments which are concerned with this problem, perhaps progress could be made. I know that Mr. Field and his officials are doing the very best job they possibly can. I know that as a member of parliament I call his office from time to time and every courtesy is extended to me. I know he is keen to help hon. members and if there is a reasonably good suggestion he will try and go along with it and help.
Limitations are placed upon him, but I hope some of these problems to which I have referred can be solved and that progress can be made because of the great importance of the travel business to us in British Columbia.
I should like to refer for a moment to an article which appeared in Time magazine, March 3 issue. It says this about the United States:
Playing the genial host, the U.S. senate last week laid out a huge welcome mat for foreign tourists anxious to visit the U.S. Passed by the senate and sent to the house of representatives for almost certain approval was a bill establishing a United States travel service, whose function will be to persuade more foreigners to visit the U.S. Provided with an initial budget of $5 million, the national tourist office will open branch offices abroad, work with private business to simplify
Supply-Northern Affairs tour arrangements and hotel accommodations, entice potential visitors with a "Tour the U.S.A." program.
The article goes on to say this:
An important task of the tourist service will be to speed up visa and entry procedures. A major irritant for foreign travellers is the U.S.'s visa requirement, a practice that all but disappeared in western Europe.
The article continues:
U.S. consulates abroad have done much to simplify visa applications.. .The whole process usually takes less than 20 minutes.
It also deals with the way in which the United States air lines have assisted the United States travel bureau in promoting this "tour United States" program. I hope we can adopt a program of this type here in Canada and even improve on it.
I have often wondered just what the Swiss people would do if we vacated this country, and what the Swiss travel people would do when they realized that they had living next to them 180 million of the world's richest people, all of them infected with the travel bug. They have developed their resources in a very fine way. We have not done so, as I indicated to the minister in my humble way yesterday and, I hope, to some degree today. I hope we can show a much greater increase in our tourist trade both in the wintertime and in the summertime in the very near future.

In past years I have been somewhat critical of the travel bureau on this vote, but I should like to acknowledge what I consider to be a great improvement in the attempt made by the bureau to present the Canadian image abroad in its true perspective I have suggested in past years that the material they have produced has been designed by and large to show Canada as a vast wilderness. In fact, I was getting concerned that so many Americans crossing the border found it surprising that we had indoor plumbing. We were being pictured abroad as a country which could only contribute cold weather, mounted policemen and ducks. I think the bureau has made considerable progress with regard to the nature of the material it has produced, not only in its publication but in the media of newspapers and television which it uses.
I should like to emphasize in all seriousness the need for a further advance in terms of showing the tourist, not only from the United States but from all the other countries, that we have a great deal more than fast running water for excellent fishing, and excellent hunting. All these things we accept as a fact in Canada. I suggest, however, that in addition to these natural resources tourists expect facilities and accommodation at least

Supply-Northern Affairs as good as those offered by competing areas. We tend to lose sight of this. We have drawn attention to our outdoor attractions without giving a clear indication that this country has many metropolitan areas where visitors can enjoy good shopping and pursue many cultural interests. I think that if we were to move even further along these lines it would further the policy of the minister and of his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I offer, as a suggestion, the proposal that we should advance still further in this direction. However, I believe that this year the bureau has shown something more of Canadian life than just the outdoor atmosphere and outdoor activities. I am sure, also, that all concerned with the activities of the bureau are encouraged by the fact that in the past two or three years they have been receiving a great deal of support from provincial bodies. All of a sudden the people of Canada have become conscious of the importance of what the activities of the bureau means to Canada and of what tourism in general means to Canada, and I think the majority of these people at their conventions are agreed that we must present a more balanced approach calling attention to all the facilities which this country has to offer rather than emphasizing one particular facet.
I close, as I began, by congratulating the bureau on what I consider to be a definite improvement and by hoping that the emphasis will continue to be on a broader Canadian picture and a wider approach to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the current session of parliament several members-perhaps I should say all members-representing fishing constituencies have made reference to some of the fishery problems in their areas. In order that the committee may see the whole picture, I shall attempt briefly to review progress during 1960-61, and to indicate some of the outstanding features of these estimates for the fiscal year 1961-62.
The role of the department is essentially one of conservation and utilization of Canadian fishery resources in the broadest sense. This role embraces everything from fundamental research in the biology of marine life to the work of our test kitchen in helping consumers to get the greatest possible benefit and enjoyment from eating fish. The various services of the department all have a part to play in this co-ordinated effort.
The department, of course, does not catch fish or market fish. We are, however, keenly interested in and concerned with the economic health of the industry. This over the long run justifies our efforts. I shall therefore refer briefly to the results achieved by the industry in 1960 and to the prospects for the current year as we see them now.
90205-6-297
Supply-Fisheries
As is so frequently the case in fisheries, the year 1960 had its successes and its disappointments. It so happens that much of the disappointment was felt in the fisheries of British Columbia. Normally, the year begins with an active herring fishery for the meal and oil markets. In recent years, whaling has commenced early in the spring. Last year, world markets for fish meal were seriously depressed following a sharp expansion in production in Peru and other countries. As a result neither the herring fishery nor the whaling operations were able to proceed in British Columbia except on a much reduced scale. The salmon fishery, while not affected by any market weakness, experienced a low phase in the cycle of production in almost all species. Total landings of salmon at some 74 million pounds were only 70 per cent of the preceding year. The halibut fishery produced an increased yield of 8 per cent but lower unit prices resulted in a 6 per cent decline in value. The depressed prices for meal and oil persisted throughout the year and it was not until late November that the fishermen and processors were able to work out a basis for production. Thus over-all landings of herring fell from 444 million pounds in 1959 to only 186 million pounds in 1960.
At this point perhaps I should say a word about the fish meal situation. In addition to the herring meal production on the Pacific coast, we produce about an equal quantity of meal on the Atlantic coast as a by-product of filleting and canning operations. Canada's total production, however, is less than 5 per cent of world production and prices to our producers are determined by an international market. For that reason, FAO's move to convene a meeting of all interested countries to examine the problems that have emerged recently in the fish meal trade was welcomed by the government. The meeting took place in Rome last month and the department, along with trade and commerce and the fishing industry, was represented. It is considered to have been a successful meeting. Substantial progress was made in analysis of the demand for fish meal and similar products, in knowledge of the alternative uses of the raw material and in the organization of intelligence services for the trade. We are hopeful that these advances may introduce a degree of stability into the market for this commodity.
Returning to the general economic health of the fishery, I am happy to report that, aside from British Columbia, our fisheries enjoyed a generally satisfactory year in 1960. The lobster fishery of the Atlantic provinces was especially productive, with over 50 million pounds landed bringing $18 million to fishermen. Good catches and improved

Supply-Fisheries
prices to the producers of salted cod brought Newfoundland fishermen as a whole their highest level of income since the union of Newfoundland with Canada. Results in the inland fisheries were also generally satisfactory.
On the market side, one of the most promising features has been the renewed strength now evident in the markets for fresh and frozen fish both in Canada and the United ago has eased. Continued expansion is evident in consumer demand, particularly for cooked and prepared fish products. The wide and attractive display of these items now in evidence in chain stores is a reflection of the rapidly improving presentation of fishery products in sales outlets. As I have indicated, prices received by fishermen for salted fish were exceptionally good during 1960. This was largely the result of low European production in 1959. Production was slightly higher in 1960 and some uncertainty now surrounds the market, in Cuba particularly. An excessive year-end carryover in the 1961 season and a consequent depression of prices are a distinct possibility. A near normal production of canned salmon in 1961 should find a ready demand both at home and in foreign markets.
In the field of research, I referred last year to the good work of the research vessel A. T. Cameron in Atlantic waters. We are now proceeding with the construction of a similar 177-foot research vessel for offshore work in the Pacific. Construction of this vessel should be completed during 1962. In addition, we are extending the facilities of the fisheries research board at Nanaimo in British Columbia, at Ellerslie in Prince Edward Island and at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and Halifax, Nova Scotia. All these new facilities will provide for more intensive work from these centres. Of particular interest in the field of exploratory fishing is the work being carried on off the Mackenzie delta in the western Arctic. Here substantial bodies of groundfish have been discovered which may have at least local commercial significance. In Hudson bay survey work off the Belcher islands has indicated that there are some Arctic char in waters hitherto considered barren.
Across the country important research projects are going forward as a basis for expansion and development of our fisheries. Some examples are the salmon behaviour studies in the open waters of the Pacific, further studies of lamprey destruction and trout rehabilitation in the great lakes, the important groundfish studies on the Atlantic banks as well as shellfish exploration and study on both coasts. Similarly, technological

research is going forward in all areas designed to improve existing fisheries and to develop new ones. In oceanography we are continuing to co-operate with other departments and agencies but with special emphasis on those factors affecting the productivity of the ocean as far as fisheries are concerned. To apply the results of scientific research is the expanding activity of the department's industrial development service. I think this is something that is of particular importance because if new knowledge gained is not applied it has limited usefulness. This service is concerned primarily with the application of new developments to fish catching and to the processing of fishery products. The service has a wide range of projects under way in all provinces. It works very closely with provincial departments of fisheries and industrial development. Working arrangements have been established with practically all provincial governments. During 1960-61 this cooperative approach was extended to Ontario and the three prairie provinces. In British Columbia projects are going forward in cooperation with the fishing industry with particular emphasis on the possibilities of developing an offshore tuna fishery and further development of the shellfish industry.
I cannot take time now to list all these projects which range from the introduction, together with the province of Nova Scotia, of plastic vessel construction to studies and recommendations for improved road transport of refrigerated fishery products. Another most important feature of the work of this service is the training courses which have been arranged for fishermen in Newfoundland, the maritime provinces, Quebec and Ontario. These courses cover a range of subjects with particular emphasis on the use of new types of fishing gear. By that I mean types of gear that may not actually be new but are new to a particular area for a particular use.
The conservation and development service of the department takes responsibility for the operation of fish hatcheries and related work in the field of fish culture. It is responsible for the biological and engineering aspects of stream clearance. It includes our efforts to combat pollution and other industrial developments which interfere with the life and growth of fish in our lakes and streams. This service of the department is also responsible for administration of regulations necessary to limit and control commercial fishery operations. A major current activity has been the expansion and strengthening of our fleet of patrol vessels. Construction has already commenced on a large 179-foot patrol vessel for Newfoundland waters and additional smaller vessels are under construction for both maritime and British Columbia

waters. I might add that the name that has been decided on for the new patrol vessel for Newfoundland is Cape Freels. Its construction has been held up a bit as the shipyard where it is being built is now on strike.
One of the highlights of 1960 was the completion and inauguration of the Robertson creek spawning channel on Vancouver island. Construction of this large scale spawning area where gravel conditions and water flow can be kept under constant control is expected to make a real contribution particularly to the production of pink salmon in this area. During the current year we will be proceeding with a somewhat similar major construction program on the Big Qualicum river, also on Vancouver island. Here control of the water flow and improvement of the spawning channel will expand the populations of pink, chum, cohoe and spring salmon. Also in British Columbia we have opened an experimental hatchery on the Nanika river designed to rehabilitate the runs of sockeye in the southern branch of the Skeena river.
In Newfoundland we have continued the transfer of salmon from Great Rattling brook to Little Rattling brook. A new fishway has been installed on the Lomond river and a survey of lakes has been made to determine fish populations and to check on industrial developments which may affect the fishery.
The transfer of disease resistant oysters from Prince Edward Island to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick has been completed with reasonably satisfactory results. The department's program of oyster seed collection in Prince Edward Island continues to show good results and gives promise of a sound commercial venture. Those responsible for lobster protection are gratified that the policy of careful protection coupled with education among fishermen is paying off through increased weight of catches.
The department is co-operating with the new Department of Forestry in joint efforts to minimize the adverse effects of d.d.t. spraying of forests where that is necessary. The use of half-strength spray in 1960 gave very encouraging results.
In the Northwest Territories arrangements have been made to open up many of the small lakes to commercial fishing on a group basis from year to year. Because of the slow growth in these lakes, they cannot withstand continuous fishing but through a rotation system it is believed an economic operation will be possible.
Last year I emphasized the work being done by the inspection service in certifying fish plants under Canadian government specifications board. During the past year, an additional 10 plants met the standard and now 41 plants have been certified. It is now 90205-6-297J
Supply-Fisheries
believed that at least 75 per cent of processed fish is being produced in accordance with this program. A number of additional plants are now making the necessary capital expenditures to meet the required specifications.
Market comments reaching the department indicate a very satisfactory level of quality both in the domestic and export markets but our goal is for still higher standards. It is obvious that if standards can be made even higher, the consumer acceptance of and desire for fish will become even greater as people recognize fish as an excellent source of food protein which is relatively economic to buy. Two new large mobile laboratories, one to service the Gaspe region and a second to be based at Winnipeg, have been acquired. As these mobile laboratories move throughout their respective areas "open house" educational programs are carried on. In addition, special courses have been put on in co-operation with provincial governments. In the current year we will be proceeding with construction of a new inspection laboratory at Halifax replacing and extending the present inadequate facilities in that area.
Courses are being arranged for fish cannery foremen in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick and similar courses will be held in St. John's, Newfoundland and Halifax, Nova Scotia for the foremen of fish processing plants. We believe these training courses are particularly valuable and we welcome requests for them from the fish processing industry.
The department through its information service and its home economics section carries on a continuing campaign to create a greater awareness of the excellent dishes that can be made from fishery products. Every month consumer releases are forwarded to newspapers and magazines and radio and television stations. Much of the material sent out is being widely used by the Canadian daily and weekly press and other media.
Last year I referred to "The Canadian Fish Cookbook" issued by the department's information service. I am happy to report that this publication sold very well and that an additional 10,000 copies in English and 5,000 copies in French have now become available for further sales.
In the 1961-62 estimates provision is made for the production of posters and a filmstrip on Atlantic salmon. These will be used to carry the message of conservation to both anglers and commercial Atlantic salmon fishermen and the general public.
In Newfoundland the serious problem of inadequate bait supplies was relieved in 1960 by a sharp increase in the availability of squid. At the same time, improved facilities

Supply-Fisheries
have been made available to the Newfoundland bait service. I have referred on previous occasions to the bait holding units which have been introduced to supplement the original supply depots. We now have 20 of these additional units and further additional units are being provided. The estimates for this year make provision for eight additional units to be added in this fiscal year. Provision is also sought to cover plans and designs of a large refrigerated vessel to replace the M.V. Arctica which is now 42 years old.
The program of constructing community stages in Newfoundland is virtually completed. The twentieth one will be constructed in Labrador during this year. I might add that discussions are under way with the government of Newfoundland with the end in view of continuing this program- of course, at a slower speed but nevertheless continuing it

into the future.
Canada, as hon. members know, is signatory to seven international fisheries conventions. Three of them are in partnership with the United States. I refer to the international Pacific halibut fisheries convention, the international Pacific salmon fisheries convention and the great lakes fisheries convention. Several countries join with us in each of the others as well as the United States.
These international fisheries agreements are of significant importance to Canada, of course. They include continuing obligations, in Canada's fisheries interest, which have been assumed by the government. In all of these conventions provision has been made for the establishment of commissions composed of representatives from each of the signatory countries. The implementation of the conventions, in so far as Canada is concerned, comes under the authority and is the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries. The government is directly represented on all the commissions by senior officials of the Department of Fisheries. All Canadian commissioners are appointed by order in council.
It was decided by the government and other governments that are parties to the conventions, particularly the more recent conventions, that the scientific investigations recommended by the commissions under coordinated programs and accepted by the governments were to be undertaken by the national agencies of the countries involved. This provision permits each country to retain its identity in the field of the investigations which it undertakes. There is no question that the scientific investigations conducted by the Department of Fisheries research agency, the fisheries research board, represent advances in scientific knowledge which would not have been gained otherwise. >
*Mr. MacLean (Queens).]
The Canadian fishing industry is heavily dependent on the sea fisheries from which comes the bulk of the Canadian production. Because of the international character of some of the most important fisheries adjacent to our coasts it is imperative that the Canadian government have scientific knowledge on which to propose any necessary conservation measures. This knowledge must be supplied by its own research facilities.
I think it is well to bear in mind the fact that, for many years, Canada has played a leading role in the development of international co-operation in fisheries matters. It is true, of course, that Canada has a direct major interest in these conventions for its own purposes, but there is also the equally important fact that the government of Canada has taken the firm position that in all fields of international relations it is only by co-operation, understanding and mutual respect that problems can be resolved and solutions found for the benefit of all nations.
I hope that the general comments I have just made, Mr. Chairman, will serve the purpose of indicating the scope of the activities of the department. We will continue, of course, to work with other departments, with provincial governments and with all branches of the industry towards an expanding and prosperous fishing industry in the years ahead.

I well recall, during the campaign of 195758, when the Prime Minister, addressing large gatherings in certain fishing areas of the Atlantic provinces, offered fishermen a fixed minimum price for their fish. This statement was made in no uncertain terms, particularly in the town of Yarmouth on March 25, 1958. The Prime Minister insisted, on that occasion, on the need for fish price supports similar to those provided for farm products, and further stated that his government would relate prices to fishermens' costs of operations. No action has been taken in this field whatever.
In the present estimates there is an increase of $3,000 for the operation or administration of the Fisheries Prices Support Act. To my mind this $3,000 is probably included to pay the increases in salaries to the staff of the fisheries prices support board and for no other reason.
This board, which has been in operation since 1957, was instituted to support prices of fisheries products, and has the power to purchase any fisheries product at a prescribed price, or to make deficiency payments to producers of fisheries products equal to the difference between the prescribed price and the alleged price at which a certain product was sold during a specified period. It is the duty of that board to maintain a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries products, and those from products of other industries.
The accomplishments of this particular board in the last five or six years have been just about negligible. I realize that in the last 10 or 12 years the Canadian government has introduced a number of assistance programs for the fishing industry, particularly since the post-war period, and I wish to outline some of these programs to show what they cost the Canadian fishermen at the present time.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I wish to thank hon. members for allowing me to carry on. As I said, the total cost of such assistance during any of the last few fiscal years amounted to approximately $1,750,000 per year. This cannot be considered at all exhorbitant for an industry which provides a livelihood for 60,000 to 75,000 primary producers and employment for another 100,000 employees engaged in the preparation of fish for market.
I am not against certain emergency measures which have to be taken care of by the federal treasury such as the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, for example, which will cost the treasury $11,800,000 during the coming fiscal year, and the subsidy

on the movement of coal amounting to $13,244,000; compensation for slaughtered animals amounting to $2,220,000, which is $750,000 more than all of the measures now in existence to assist the fishermen.
The time seems to have come for practical and definite action on the part of the De-parment of Fisheries for the benefit and the expansion of the industry. As was brought out at the fisheries council meeting held in Toronto a few weeks ago, prospects of the fishing industry in the immediate future are not too bright. When one realizes that the Canadian consumption of fish which had reached 13.7 pounds per capita in 1950 was down to 13.2 pounds in 1957, one must admit that something drastic should be done to increase the consumption of fish on the domestic market.
