I said that in 1950 the consumption of fish in Canada amounted to 13.7 pounds per capita. In 1957, seven years later, it was down to 13.2 pounds per capita.
It is most unfortunate that such an important industry, an industry which is so vital to our general economy, and particularly to the economy of the Atlantic provinces, must depend on the export market for the sale of over 80 per cent of its production. It is understandable that an organization like the fisheries council, which has spent $184,000 since 1953 in trying to promote the consumption of fish, particularly in our domestic market, is now reluctant to further support and assist such a promotion program. The efforts of the fisheries council of the past seven years must not be wasted, and the federal government should come to the assistance of the council in no uncertain way to promote and develop the consumption of fish in our domestic market.
The activities of the department in this particular field, in co-operation with the Department of Trade and Commerce, should not be limited to domestic consumption but should be diverted, and in no uncertain way, to the advertising of our Canadian fisheries products abroad.
The department should pay particular attention to the present situation of our salt fish market, which is going through a very critical time. The present position of our salt fish stocks in the Atlantic provinces could seriously affect the returns of our fishermen at the opening of the present fishing season.
Another important factor which should concern the federal government and which is strongly recommended by the fisheries council is the recognition of the same rights of Canadian fishermen as those enjoyed by foreign 90205-6-298
Supply-Fisheries
fishermen operating in eastern Canadian waters. The bill which was introduced in the house on May 2 does take care of the situation to a certain extent, but I suggest also that consideration should be given to protecting not only the fishermen operating the larger trawlers but also the owners of small vessels operating in what is commonly known as inshore water. I have in mind definite regulations which might be applied, not just on paper as they are often applied at the present time, prohibiting the operation of certain trawlers in certain portions of waters which should be limited to inshore fishermen. The minister is vested with all the authority required to apply such a regulation by section 7 of the otter trawler fishing regulations established by order in council on May 6, 1951.
Such regulations, for example, have been made to apply to operations of certain sizes of trawlers or draggers of limited length in certain portions of the Baie de Chaleur. Unfortunately, these regulations are being enforced by the department as they should be and consequently a number of fishermen on certain sections of the Baie de Chaleur operating small fishing boats are being interfered with by larger draggers from New Brunswick and the Quebec side of the bay. I urge the minister to take proper steps to have his officials enforce the existing regulations and, if need be, amend them in order to protect the inshore fishermen of that particular area of the bay.
In introducing his estimates on June 29 of last year, the minister referred to limited advertising on the part of his department which had met with very good consumer response, and he referred again tonight to this advertising program. I realize that in this instance he was making particular reference to the "Canada inspected" or "Canada approved" program which began on April 1, 1959, and which has been expanding ever since. I know we are all pleased to hear that the number of plants that have qualified under this program has increased from 10 to 40 in the last fiscal year. There is no doubt that the consumers of first quality products, as well as the fishing industry, cannot help but benefit from the sale of a product which bears the inscription "Canada inspected", or "Processed under government supervision". The work of the department in this field of action must be activated and its inspection personnel must be given the opportunity to qualify themselves for this very complicated and delicate job.
This does not mean, however, that the department must limit itself to the limited advertising of fishery products. The consumer service of the department must be

Supply-Fisheries
expanded in such a way as to show results which will aim at increased fish consumption in our domestic market. There is ample room for improvement in this field of advertising and I urge the minister to take meas-sures to improve and expand his department's participation in his general consumer advertising so that the consumption of fish may increase.

At no time have I criticized increased expenditures by the department. I said that I welcomed increased expenditures provided results were achieved, provided there was an increase in catch and an increase in revenue for our fishermen, and provided we could show an increase in the marketing of our fish.
For the last two years, Mr. Chairman, we have had in my home town of Caraquet a fisheries school. A few weeks ago I attended the closing of a class of 30 fishermen and sons of fishermen who had completed their second year of a course in fisheries. The interest has been of such a wide magnitude that the facilities provided by the Caraquet school board are now inadequate and the need has been established for a new building which could provide the necessary classrooms and other facilities for the first school of its kind in the Atlantic provinces.
In fact, the government of the province of New Brunswick announced a few weeks ago its decision to proceed in co-operation with the federal government with the construction of this new school under the technical and vocational training assistance program. I wish to express at this time my full appreciation for the application of this vocational training program which, according to the Minister of Labour's own words, will include all training of all sorts and types below the university level.
I would express the hope that the new school when in operation will receive better co-operation from the Department of Fisheries than has been extended so far to the present school in its first two years of existence. The department has failed to give the present school the technical assistance which it was in a position to offer. It has reluctantly agreed, and this after all kinds of reservations and hesitation, to allow some members of its staff to take part in the kind of instruction which was required to provide the students with adequate information relating to the handling and preparation of fish.

I will admit that such educational work does not come within the immediate duties of departmental officials. I will also admit that the department and particularly the fisheries research board have provided some services which have been appreciated by the director of the school, the teaching staff and students alike. But it would have been much more profitable to all concerned if less hesitation and better understanding had existed on the part of the department, thus showing its full willingness to co-operate in the success of a new venture which had as its immediate goal the success and development of our fishing industry.
I would urge the minister to consider the possibility of increasing in next year's estimates the item covering educational work in fisheries techniques and co-operative producing and selling among fishermen. The present school of fisheries at Caraquet and particularly the new school which should open its doors in 1962 or early 1963 will be directly concerned with educational work in fisheries' techniques. I note with interest that in this year's estimates this item shows an additional $25,000 grant to Memorial university in St. John's, Newfoundland. I welcome this grant which will contribute to the further development of fisheries' knowledge or research in an area where fishing is of such vital importance. I hope the minister will keep in mind similar assistance measures for the new fisheries school which will be established in Caraquet next year.

I am sure the committee was also extremely interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester. What the minister and the hon. member for Gloucester have said will be of invaluable assistance to the committee in considering the various items in the estimates of the department. There may be disagreement on the interpretation of various statistics that have been introduced but nevertheless I am sure what they have said will be of great benefit to us.
Generally speaking, I find that the fishermen have a high degree of admiration for the activities of the Department of Fisheries. They may complain on occasion about specific phases of its operations but generally I think they have this feeling and in my view it is well justified. With regard to the minister's reference to increases respecting the fisheries

research board, these are most welcome, of course, because we feel that in the activities of the board we may find the solution to many of the problems confronting the various fisheries in Canada.
I should also like to pay my respects publicly to Dr. Kask and his staff of the research board for the outstanding work they have done with the somewhat limited resources at their disposal. Dr. Kask lived for a long period of time on the Queen Charlotte islands in the constituency I represent. He was well thought of and well liked while he was there and I am quite sure that those same feelings still exist and will continue to exist wherever he happens to be. I wonder whether I might call it ten thirty.

speechtext: I am very happy to rise following a question from the opposition on this matter. On Monday and Tuesday we will be dealing with legislation. Frankly I am not in a position at the moment to detail the legislation with which we will be dealing.
